## Introduction

Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) are a large and ancient family of small, non-enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses that establish infection in stratified squamous epithelia. More than 220 HPV types have now been fully sequenced and formally classified, partitioned by L1 open-reading-frame identity into five genera: *Alpha-*, *Beta-*, *Gamma-*, *Mu-* and *Nupapillomavirus* [@devilliers2004; @bzhalava2015]. This genus structure tracks tissue tropism and disease association: the alpha genus contains the mucosal, sexually transmitted types responsible for cervical and other anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers (HPV16, HPV18), whereas the great majority of described types are cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs whose natural habitat is the skin [@devilliers2004; @vandoorslaer2017]. Despite outnumbering the medically prominent alpha types, these cutaneous viruses remain comparatively poorly characterized, and the curated reference genomes that make systematic study possible are consolidated in the Papillomavirus Episteme (PaVE; @vandoorslaer2017).

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs behave less like classical pathogens than like members of the commensal skin flora. They are acquired in early life, are ubiquitous on the skin of healthy immunocompetent adults, and persist for months to years as asymptomatic, often low-level infections [@antonsson2000]. Culture-independent surveys of normal-appearing skin reveal striking inter-individual diversity, with multiple co-resident beta- and gamma-genotypes and a continuing discovery of novel types from healthy skin [@foulongne2012; @nunes2018]. At DNA level this reservoir is both large and well mapped: shotgun metagenomics of the Human Microbiome Project found HPV in 61.3% of skin samples from healthy subjects, the highest of any body site surveyed [@ma2014], and type-specific PCR of skin swabs detects beta-HPV in 92% and gamma-HPV in 84% of adults undergoing skin-cancer screening [@rollison2019sites]. Deep sequencing of skin has extended the catalog to 396 HPV types, 229 of them previously unknown [@bzhalava2014], so the reservoir is also substantially larger than any reference panel describes. What these DNA-based figures cannot say is whether any of that genetic material is being transcribed. In immunocompetent hosts this carriage is overwhelmingly subclinical: most cutaneous HPV infection lies in a "twilight zone" of latency and immune control rather than producing visible lesions [@doorbar2023]. Yet the composition and frequency of this reservoir in healthy skin remain a basic, incompletely answered descriptive question: which types are actually present, and how often?

A minority of cutaneous infections do become overtly productive and lesional, and two settings define this productive extreme. Common, plantar and flat warts are highly productive infections, driven principally by alpha types HPV2, HPV27 and HPV57, the mu type HPV1, and gamma types such as HPV4, in which abundant virion assembly in the differentiating epidermis produces the koilocytes that are the histological signature of active viral replication [@egawa2017]. Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV), or Lewandowsky–Lutz dysplasia, is the second: a rare genodermatosis of selective susceptibility to beta-HPVs that manifests as lifelong flat-wart and pityriasis-versicolor-like lesions, with progression to cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) on sun-exposed skin [@orth2006; @dejong2018a]. EV is a Mendelian "experiment of nature": biallelic loss-of-function in the adjacent keratinocyte genes *EVER1*/*EVER2* (*TMC6*/*TMC8*), and subsequently in *CIB1*, abolishes a keratinocyte-intrinsic restriction of beta-HPV and renders these otherwise-quiescent commensals pathogenic [@ramoz2002; @lazarczyk2008; @dejong2018b]. Warts and EV thus provide the natural positive controls for high-burden, transcriptionally active cutaneous HPV infection.

Between asymptomatic carriage and frank lesion lies the most consequential and most contested role of beta-HPV: as a cofactor in the development of cSCC, the second most common human cancer. Beta-HPV is detected at high frequency in actinic keratoses (AK) and cSCC, particularly in organ-transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed patients, whose cSCC risk is elevated many-fold [@howley2015; @rollison2019]. The mechanistic model that reconciles this association with the virus's commensal nature is the "hit-and-run" hypothesis: beta-HPV acts early, cooperating with ultraviolet (UV) radiation to expand a field of damaged keratinocytes, but is dispensable for maintenance of the established tumour. Beta-HPV E6 proteins impair the cellular response to UV damage, abrogating ATR signaling and the repair of UV-induced lesions, and disrupt NOTCH and TGF-β signaling to sustain proliferation, without degrading p53 as high-risk alpha-HPV does [@wallace2012; @meyers2017]. Direct experimental support comes from transgenic and infection models in which genetic deletion of the viral oncogenes after lesions have formed, or transplantation of secondary tumours, leaves carcinoma growth unaffected and viral genomes undetectable [@viarisio2018; @dorfer2021], and from UV-dependent MmuPV1 skin carcinogenesis in mice [@uberoi2016]. Consistent with hit-and-run, viral load and transcription in human tissue are highest in early precursor lesions and decline in established carcinoma [@borgogna2018]. This view is not unchallenged. T-cell immunity to commensal papillomaviruses has been shown to be actively *protective* against skin carcinogenesis, reframing immunosuppression-associated cSCC as a failure of antiviral immunosurveillance rather than direct viral oncogenesis [@strickley2019]; that claim drew a formal Matters Arising from the opposing camp and a reply [@lambert2021; @strickley2021], and the exchange remains unresolved. Two developments since have made the contest less tractable rather than more. First, the protective-immunity account now predicts the same longitudinal pattern as hit-and-run: in UV-damaged skin, papillomavirus colonization blocks the expansion of mutant p53 clones in a CD8^+^ T-cell-dependent manner, beta-HPV activity is elevated in sun-exposed human skin carrying such clones, and the expansion of those clones in premalignant lesions is associated with *loss* of beta-HPV [@son2025]. A decline in viral activity along the progression axis is therefore a prediction of both models, not a signature of either. Second, a purely virological explanation for quiescence exists alongside both: the beta-HPV genome represses its own gene expression and replication through the viral E8\^E2 protein, and immortalization of human keratinocytes by a beta-HPV genome requires that repressor to be inactivated [@rehm2022], so transcriptional quiet may be the cis-encoded default state of the virus rather than a statement about immunity or tumour biology. What is missing from this debate is not another mechanism but a measurement: how often, and how actively, cutaneous HPV is actually transcribed across the spectrum from healthy skin to carcinoma.

Resolving these questions requires distinguishing productive infection from latent, abortive, or transformed states, and the viral transcriptional program provides exactly this readout. The papillomavirus life cycle is obligately coupled to keratinocyte differentiation: early genes (*E1*, *E2*, *E5*, *E6*, *E7*) are expressed in basal and proliferating cells, whereas genome amplification and the late capsid genes (*L1*, *L2*) are activated only in the terminally differentiated suprabasal layers, where virions are assembled and shed [@doorbar2012; @graham2017]. This temporal order is enforced by differentiation-dependent promoter switching, alternative splicing and a shift from early to late polyadenylation [@johansson2013]. Detection of late (L1/L2) capsid transcripts is consequently a hallmark of productive infection, and can be read out directly from RNA sequencing [@klymenko2017; @borgogna2014]. The contrast is sharpest in cancer: when HPV integrates, the late program, and frequently *E2*, is lost, leaving deregulated *E6*/*E7* as the dominant viral transcripts [@moody2010]. Integration itself is not a single state, and reading it from transcription rather than presence is what separates its variants: multi-omic profiling of cervical cancer distinguishes silent from productive integration sites by whether they generate viral-host fusion transcripts, finds only the productive class non-randomly distributed and associated with higher E6/E7 protein and more aggressive disease, and shows the productive fraction rising from carcinoma in situ to advanced disease [@fan2023]. An early-versus-late transcript signature therefore separates the productive warts and EV lesions from the latent carriage of normal skin and from any non-productive footprint in carcinoma.

These questions are, in principle, already answerable from data that exist. Public sequence archives now hold millions of human RNA-seq libraries, and re-mining this resource has repeatedly recovered viral signal that the original studies ignored [@edgar2022]. The obstacle is a near-universal feature of transcriptomic pipelines: reads that do not map to the human genome are discarded at the outset, so any HPV transcripts present are silently filtered away before analysis. Recovering them requires returning to the raw reads and classifying the non-human fraction explicitly, an approach validated by dedicated virus-detection workflows [@yasumizu2021] and efficient metagenomic classifiers such as Kraken2 [@wood2019]. Skin is no exception. Screening the off-target reads of commonly available sequencing data across 19 skin tumour types identified HPV42 as the driver of digital papillary adenocarcinoma, present in 96% of cases [@leiendecker2023], and a multidimensional reprocessing of 8,274 public skin RNA-seq samples from 132 experiments recovered bacterial, protist and viral RNA including HPV among the skin flora it cataloged [@bhargava2025]. Neither discarded-read mining of skin nor its application at archive scale is therefore new; what has not been done is to use it to estimate how often cutaneous HPV is present, which types, and whether the infection is productive. Whether cutaneous HPV is transcriptionally active in skin cancer has in fact been asked directly, by several groups and on several platforms, and the answers converge. Transcriptome sequencing of cSCC concluded that HPV is "not active" in these tumours [@arron2011]; total RNA sequencing of 12 skin lesions, 11 of them HPV DNA-positive, recovered transcripts from one, at a median of 66 million reads [@hultin2019]; whole-transcriptome analysis of 345 post-transplant non-melanoma skin cancers at a median of 35 million reads found HPV transcription in 15 [@arroyomuhr2021]; RNA sequencing of 23 risk-stratified cSCC and normal-skin biopsies found no HPV expression at all, against 64% HPV DNA positivity in the same series [@vandiver2021]; and E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization across 243 cutaneous SCC detected high-risk transcripts in 0.9% of the 225 non-anogenital cases [@fujimoto2019]. The convergence is not total: an earlier in situ study found EV-HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 PCR-positive transplant-recipient cSCC, localized to the mid and upper epidermis [@purdie2005], and whole-transcriptome virome profiling reads cutaneous HPV transcripts readily from EV skin [@saeidian2023]. What no study has yet done is put the question on a denominator large enough, and a control series wide enough, to say what the population-level answer is: the transcriptomic series above run from 11 to 345 specimens, four of the five are confined to lesional tissue with no unselected-skin comparator, the largest is exclusively immunosuppressed and formalin-fixed, and the one covering the widest range of cutaneous types scores transcription of any viral gene rather than productive replication. The question is therefore not whether HPV transcripts can be found in cutaneous neoplasia, which is settled, but at what rate they occur across the skin spectrum, whether they represent productive infection, and how they compare with a lesion in which productive infection is certain. Any such effort must also contend with contamination: the HeLa cell line carries integrated HPV18 and is a pervasive source of spurious HPV18 (and HPV16/HPV38) reads in public datasets, propagated through shared reagents and index hopping [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013]. Distinguishing genuine infection from contaminant signal demands coverage-breadth and read-count thresholds, careful flagging of cell-line and engineered samples, and normalization for sequencing depth so that apparent "burden" is not merely a function of how deeply a library was sequenced.

Here we systematically re-mine public human RNA-seq data to characterize the cutaneous HPV transcriptome across tissues and disease states, applying a uniform pipeline that screens every library for papillomavirus reads, types the positives against the full PaVE reference set, and classifies their early-versus-late transcriptional activity. We frame the analysis as a case/control design spanning productive controls (warts and EV), the unselected-skin null, and the open question of HPV-associated skin neoplasia (AK and cSCC), with cell-line and contamination signals identified and depth-normalized throughout. In doing so we address four questions: (1) which HPV types are prevalent in healthy human skin; (2) which HPV types are associated with the spectrum of skin pathology; (3) in which non-traditional tissues HPV transcripts can be detected; and (4) in which transcriptomes the virus reaches the productive (late-transcript) phase of its life cycle. The first and third of these have been answered at DNA level, by body-site metagenomic mapping of healthy carriage [@ma2014]; what is asked here is the transcriptional counterpart, which is a different quantity and, as the results show, a much smaller one.
